{{Short description|Mathematical theorem regarding operators}}

In mathematics, '''Blackwell's contraction mapping theorem''' provides a set of sufficient conditions for an operator to be a [[contraction mapping]]. It is widely used in areas that rely on [[dynamic programming]] as it facilitates the proof of existence of fixed points. The result is due to [[David Blackwell]] who published it <ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/2238089 Blackwell, David. “Discounted Dynamic Programming.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 36, no. 1 (1965): 226–35. R, http://www.jstor.org/stable/2238089. Accessed 15 Aug. 2022.]</ref> in 1965 in the [[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]].

== Statement of the Theorem ==

Let <math>T</math> be an operator defined over an [[Normed vector space|ordered normed vector space]] <math>X</math>. <math>T: X \rightarrow X</math> is a contraction mapping with modulus <math>\beta</math> if it satisfies
# <math> (monotonicity) \quad u \leq v \implies Tu \leq Tv </math>
# <math> (discounting)  \quad T(u+c) \leq Tu+\beta c. </math>

== Proof of the Theorem ==

For all <math>u</math> and <math>v \in X</math>, <math>u \leq v + ||v-u||</math>. Properties 1. and 2. imply that <math>T(v) \leq T(u + ||v-u||) \leq T(u) + \beta ||v-u||</math>, hence, <math>T(v)-T(u) \leq \beta ||v-u||</math>.
Therefore <math>||T(v)-T(u)|| \leq \beta ||v-u|| </math> and  <math>T </math> is a [[contraction mapping]].

== Illustration ==

If <math>X </math> is the [[Number line|real line]] with the usual order structure and <math> T: X \rightarrow X </math> is a differentiable map satisfying <math> 0 \leq T'(x) \leq \beta <1 </math>, then <math> T </math> satisfies the assumption because <math> T'(x) >0 </math> is equivalent to monotonicity and because the derivative assumption implies with the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]] that the discounting assumption <math> T(u+c) =T(u) + \int_0^c T'(t) \; dt \leq \int_0^c \beta \; dt = Tu+\beta c </math> holds. The conclusion of the Blackwell's contraction mapping theorem is that <math>T </math> is a contraction. While this is not an impressive conclusion in the context of calculus, it is notable that the theorem does not make any differentiability assumption. The discounting assumption however implies that T is [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]]. 

== Applications ==

=== The cake eating problem ===

An agent has access to only one cake for its entire, infinite, life. It has to decide the optimal way to consume it. It evaluates a consumption plan, <math>c_t</math>, by using a separable utility function, <math>\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t \frac{c_t^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}</math>, with discounting factor <math>\beta \in (0,1)</math>. Its problem can be summarized as

<math> \max_{c_t}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t \frac{c_t^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} \text{ subject to }  x_t = x_{t-1} - c_t \text{, } x_{-1}=1 \text{, }c_t\geq0 \text{ and } x_t \geq 0 \, \forall \, t \, \in \, \mathbb{Z}_+  </math>. ({{EquationRef|1}})

Applying Bellman's principle of optimality we find ({{EquationNote|1}})'s corresponding [[Bellman equation]]

<math> V(c) = \max_{c' \in [0, c]} \frac{{c'}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta V(c - c') </math>. ({{EquationRef|2}})

It can be proven that the solution to this functional equation, if it exists, is equivalent to the solution of ({{EquationNote|1}}).<ref>Stokey, Nancy L., Robert E. Lucas, and Edward C. Prescott. Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics. Harvard University Press, 1989. https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvjnrt76.</ref> To prove its existence we can resort to Blackwell's sufficient conditions.

Define the operator <math> T(V(c)) = \sup_{c'} \frac{c^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta V(c - c') </math>. A solution to  ({{EquationNote|2}}) is equivalent to finding a fixed-point for our operator. If we prove that this operator is a contraction mapping then we can use [[Banach fixed-point theorem|Banach's fixed-point theorem]], and conclude that there is indeed a solution to ({{EquationNote|1}}).

Note that <math>T</math> is defined over the space <math> X </math> of bounded functions on <math> [0,1] </math>, and maps bounded functions to bounded functions. Notice that the desired value function for our problem is clearly bounded. Endowing <math> X </math> with the [[sup-norm]] we conclude that the domain and co-domain are ordered normed vector spaces. We are just left with verifying that the conditions for Blackwell's theorem are respected:
#(monotonicity) <math> \text{if }V(c) \geq U(c) \, \forall \, c \, \in \, [0,1]</math> then  <math> T(V(c)) = \max_{c'} \frac{{c'}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta V(c - c') \geq  \max_{c'} \frac{{c'}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta U(c - c') = T(U(c)) </math>
#(discounting)  <math> T(V(c)+a) = \max_{c'} \frac{{c'}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta (V(c - c') + a) \leq \max_{c'} \frac{{c'}^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma} + \beta V(c - c') + \beta a = T(V(c)) + \beta a </math> where <math>a</math> is a constant function.
